books.section: Topic 4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture, B. The Market Revolution's Impact on Economic Class

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Barron’s Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.6 B: In the 1830s, the mill workers in Lowell, Massachusetts, staged two strikes. In 1834, the women staged an unsuccessful “turn-out” to protest a wage cut. Two years later, organized as the Factory Girls Association, they had greater success protesting a rent increase in the boardinghouses. In 1842, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court decided Commonwealth v. Hunt, declaring that unions were lawful organizations as long as they used legal means — including striking — to achieve their goals.
stimulus.source_note: Secondary text: paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.6 B. Paraphrased, not quoted.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The Lowell mill women organized and struck in the 1830s mainly to

options.text: demand the right to vote in state elections
options.misconception: The mill women struck over pay and rent, not the vote; women could not vote in this period.

options.text: end slavery in the Southern states
options.misconception: The Lowell strikes were about mill conditions, not abolition, which was a separate reform cause.

options.text: defend their pay and living conditions against cuts
close the mills and return to farming
options.misconception: The women struck to keep their mill jobs on fair terms, not to close the mills.

rationales.A: The vote was not their demand. They struck over a wage cut in 1834 and a rent increase in 1836.
rationales.B: Abolition was a separate cause. The Factory Girls Association organized mill workers around mill conditions.
rationales.C: The passage names the two strikes: the 1834 turn-out against a wage cut and the 1836 protest against higher boardinghouse rents. Both were defenses of pay and living conditions.
rationales.D: A strike stops work to win terms, not to end the work. The women wanted fair pay and rents, not closed mills.
rationales.general:
1. Name the two strikes. A turn-out against a wage cut in 1834, and a protest against higher rents in 1836.
2. Ask what both defend. Pay and living conditions, the two things a mill worker lives on.
3. Answer from the passage. They organized to defend what they had, not to win the vote or end slavery.
Background: The women organized as the Factory Girls Association, one of the first unions of women workers in America.
Remember: a strike's cause is in what it protests, so read the grievance.
